breach.name: DominosIndia
breach.title: Domino's India
breach.summary: In April 2021, 13TB of compromised Domino's India appeared for sale on a hacking forum after which the company acknowledged a major data breach they dated back to March. The compromised data included 22.5 million unique email addresses, names, phone numbers, order histories and physical addresses.

background: In April 2021, 13TB of compromised Domino's India appeared for sale on a hacking forum after which the company acknowledged a major data breach they dated back to March. The compromised data included 22.5 million unique email addresses, names, phone numbers, order histories and physical addresses.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 22,527,655 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Purchases.
editorial: An order history attached to a delivery address and a phone number is not retail data, it is a behavioural record. Where you live, roughly when you are home, how often you order, how much you spend and how many people you are ordering for. Twenty-two and a half million of those, from a company most customers thought of as a way to get dinner.

What made this breach notorious in India was what happened after it: a public search interface was built on top of the data, so that anyone could type a phone number and read back the orders and addresses attached to it. That step is the one worth remembering. A dump on a forum has a small audience with some technical patience; a search box has everybody.

The same records become a different kind of danger when the barrier drops from "can navigate a hacking forum" to "can type". The fraud that follows is the refund call, and it works because the caller opens with a real order. Something went wrong with your last delivery, we are processing a refund, approve the request on your phone.

No merchant in India or anywhere else returns money by asking you to approve a UPI collect request or read out a one-time code, a refund travels back along the payment that made it, with nothing required from you.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Purchases
fields.why: What was bought and when, detail that makes an impersonation convincing.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
breach.scale_line: That is about 83% of the population of Australia.
